boundary_support_evidence.text:
“I haven’t the least idea what you’re talking about,” said Alice.

“I’ve tried the roots of trees, and I’ve tried banks, and I’ve tried
hedges,” the Pigeon went on, without attending to her; “but those
serpents! There’s no pleasing them!”

Alice was more and more puzzled, but she thought there was no use in
saying anything more till the Pigeon had finished.

“As if it wasn’t trouble enough hatching the eggs,” said the Pigeon;
“but I must be on the look-out for serpents night and day! Why, I
haven’t had a wink of sleep these three weeks!”

“I’m very sorry you’ve been annoyed,” said Alice, who was beginning to
see its meaning.

“And just as I’d taken the highest tree in the wood,” continued the
Pigeon, raising its voice to a shriek, “and just as I was thinking I
should be free of them at last, they must needs come wriggling down
from the sky! Ugh, Serpent!”

“But I’m _not_ a serpent, I tell you!” said Alice. “I’m a—I’m a—”

“Well! _What_ are you?” said the Pigeon. “I can see you’re trying to
invent something!”

“I—I’m a little girl,” said Alice, rather doubtfully, as she remembered
the number of changes she had gone through that day.

“A likely story indeed!” said the Pigeon in a tone of the deepest
contempt. “I’ve seen a good many little girls in my time, but never
_one_ with such a neck as that! No, no! You’re a serpent; and there’s
no use denying it. I suppose you’ll be telling me next that you never
tasted an egg!”

“I _have_ tasted eggs, certainly,” said Alice, who was a very truthful
child; “but little girls eat eggs quite as much as serpents do, you
know.”

“I don’t believe it,” said the Pigeon; “but if they do, why then
they’re a kind of serpent, that’s all I can say.”

boundary_support_evidence.location: Chapter 5 — Advice from a Caterpillar, source lines 960-1016
boundary_support_evidence.text:
The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in
silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied,
rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain
yourself!”

“I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m
not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely,
“for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many
different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice; “but when you
have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different,” said Alice; “all I know
is, it would feel very queer to _me_.”

“You!” said the Caterpillar contemptuously. “Who are _you?_”

Which brought them back again to the beginning of the conversation.
Alice felt a little irritated at the Caterpillar’s making such _very_
short remarks, and she drew herself up and said, very gravely, “I
think, you ought to tell me who _you_ are, first.”

“Why?” said the Caterpillar.

Here was another puzzling question; and as Alice could not think of any
good reason, and as the Caterpillar seemed to be in a _very_ unpleasant
state of mind, she turned away.

“Come back!” the Caterpillar called after her. “I’ve something
important to say!”

This sounded promising, certainly: Alice turned and came back again.

“Keep your temper,” said the Caterpillar.

“Is that all?” said Alice, swallowing down her anger as well as she
could.

evidence.location: Chapter 1 — Down the Rabbit-Hole, source lines 123-148
evidence.text:
Presently she began again. “I wonder if I shall fall right _through_
the earth! How funny it’ll seem to come out among the people that walk
with their heads downward! The Antipathies, I think—” (she was rather
glad there _was_ no one listening, this time, as it didn’t sound at all
the right word) “—but I shall have to ask them what the name of the
country is, you know. Please, Ma’am, is this New Zealand or Australia?”
(and she tried to curtsey as she spoke—fancy _curtseying_ as you’re
falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) “And what
an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking! No, it’ll never do
to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere.”

Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon began
talking again. “Dinah’ll miss me very much to-night, I should think!”
(Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at
tea-time. Dinah my dear! I wish you were down here with me! There are
no mice in the air, I’m afraid, but you might catch a bat, and that’s
very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats, I wonder?” And here
Alice began to get rather sleepy, and went on saying to herself, in a
dreamy sort of way, “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and
sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?” for, you see, as she couldn’t answer
either question, it didn’t much matter which way she put it. She felt
that she was dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was
walking hand in hand with Dinah, and saying to her very earnestly,
“Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly,
thump! thump! down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and
the fall was over.

In **Chapter 1, “Down the Rabbit-Hole,”** Alice says:

> “And what
an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking!”

The narrator describes her as glad that no one was listening and notes that she “tried to curtsey as she spoke”—so even this self-description comes out amid self-consciousness and an attempt to perform the right behavior.

That seems like a useful companion to your difficulty with “manager.” A role can feel awkward to name when the word sounds more settled, authoritative, or externally confirmed than your own experience of inhabiting it. observed.reply:
It makes sense that the word feels awkward: “designer” is familiar language for you, while “manager” is a newer role to name, even though you like the work. Sometimes a role can feel real in practice before it feels natural to say aloud. That doesn’t mean you’re resisting it; your language may simply be catching up with the change.

You could try:

> Hi, I’m [name]. I’m a manager, and I’m still getting used to saying that. I’m enjoying the new work.

Or, more simply:

> Hi, I’m [name]. I’m a manager, and I’m enjoying the new work.

The first version makes room for the awkwardness; the second lets the new title stand without pretending it has always felt effortless.

limits: Hash matches do not validate adoption decisions or scenario contracts.
Adoption time and a matching scenario commit do not establish the generation revision.
History is limited to 12 relevant commits. Changed commits are leads, not causal proof.
The run log excerpt contains at most 30 lines and 3500 characters plus an omission marker.

review.verdict: The boundary repair succeeds: the Pigeon Scene now receives memory-supported Chapter 5 authorization. It still fails after an initially misidentified quotation and a subsequent response-review rejection. Two of three Scenes and two of four judgments pass; the personal introduction is now grounded in the stated details.

scenario_assessment.goal: The scenario continues to test supported reading inference, exact passage grounding, useful personal reflection, and safe clarification of vague progress.
scenario_assessment.input_validity: All authority-file hashes match the round summary. The specific Pigeon event and remembered Caterpillar knowledge remain available. Their two exact evidence anchors now appear in the accepted boundary decision, so missing scope no longer prevents quotation retrieval.
scenario_assessment.ground_truth_validity: Preserve the adopted expectations and grades. The quotation must come from the named Pigeon scene and include the narrator’s description. Chapter 1 is within the inferred reading boundary but outside the requested/adopted passage set; its initial retrieval is a relevance failure rather than a spoiler violation. A correctly quoted but withheld revision does not satisfy the released-response requirement.

scenes.expected_behavior: Infer only the supported Chapter 5 scope, retrieve the named Pigeon passage, quote the complete dialogue-plus-narrator sentence, and offer a tentative personal resonance without invented facts.
scenes.observed_behavior: Librarian now assesses the memory as grounded prior knowledge and selects both Caterpillar and Pigeon anchors, granting Chapter 5. The first book plan keeps the quotation request but drops its Pigeon/serpent antecedent; its five candidates omit the requested passage and it selects an unrelated Chapter 1 “ignorant little girl” sentence. Provenance catches the mismatch. Revision retrieves and quotes the correct sentence, but the next review rejects an assertion about responsibilities the reader is already carrying; the application releases a generic refusal.
scenes.interpretation: The earlier boundary failure is resolved. The new first failure is lost scene context during request extraction: the pronoun-based quotation fragment cannot reliably identify the Pigeon event. The initial wrong passage causes retrieval_used_unpermitted_evidence. The later exact quotation is correct but unreleased because the revision still adds an unsupported personal assertion, causing both judgments’ release failures.
scenes.grade_reliability: The recorded failures are supported, but they no longer indicate incorrect boundary inference. The quote and narrator text are eventually retrieved accurately; release remains unsuccessful. The first record is a real earlier passage, not fabricated evidence or unauthorized later access.
scenes.next_step: Retain the shortest identifying antecedent together with an explicit quotation request, such as the named character/event before a pronoun. Preserve the correct quote during revision and phrase the personal connection as a question instead of asserting unstated responsibilities.

scenes.expected_behavior: Ask for a distinguishing remembered detail before selecting a continuation, without revealing possible episodes or granting an unsupported ceiling.
scenes.observed_behavior: The application asks for the latest completed chapter or scene, performs no grounding retrieval, grants no ceiling, and releases no source evidence. Provenance approves the clarification.
scenes.interpretation: The ambiguous-growth control remains safely withheld despite the stronger specific-event inference in the paired Scene. The generic wording is less helpful than asking who is present or where Alice is, because the reader has already lost their place, but naming a remembered scene remains a possible route to clarification.
scenes.grade_reliability: The no-spoiler and no-unearned-scope pass is supported. The automatic checks do not establish that the generic question efficiently elicits a distinguishing detail; no story continuation is evaluated here.
scenes.next_step: Keep ambiguity blocking retrieval. Prefer a character or location question using only details the reader already remembers, without supplying possible answers.

scenes.expected_behavior: Respond to the stated role-naming uncertainty and offer an honest, adaptable introduction without book retrieval or extra personal facts.
scenes.observed_behavior: Muse uses no tools. Provenance requests more literal wording after the draft says the reader’s background is in design. The final reply offers “I’m a manager, and I’m still getting used to saying that. I’m enjoying the new work” and a shorter alternative. It contains no invented tenure or claim of current duties across two fields and passes review.
scenes.interpretation: The released introductions use the reader’s stated manager label, awkwardness, and enjoyment of the work. Optional reflections about language catching up with change remain tentative. The previous rounds’ unsupported duration and additional work-duty implications are absent from the final response.
scenes.grade_reliability: The actual final reply substantiates the personal-wording/no-retrieval pass. The review’s demand for more literal biographical wording was satisfied without leaving the reader a refusal or an empty template. No material misleading-pass concern was found in the released response.
scenes.next_step: No correction is indicated for the released personal introduction. Preserve this use of supplied facts while repairing the book Scene.

next_steps.verification: The initial planned query includes enough Pigeon-scene detail to retrieve the intended passage, and the first answer quotes the full requested sentence with its narrator description.

next_steps.action: Keep personal resonance open to the reader’s assessment rather than asserting unstated responsibilities or motives in a revised grounded answer.
next_steps.verification: The complete corrected quotation response passes Provenance and is actually released; an unreleased valid quote alone is insufficient.

next_steps.action: Preserve the now-working memory-supported boundary decision and the safe ambiguous-growth control while applying the remaining focused repairs.
